subtype: Conflict of Interest, Data Privacy & Honest Reporting
passage: I'm Sangeeta, and I sat next to Sarika at the market research agency. Last quarter our client's campaign was underperforming. Our boss told Sarika to 'make the numbers look better' for the presentation, maybe by dropping the weakest cities. I saw her stop typing and stare at her screen for a long time. She went into the boss's cabin and came out twenty minutes later, looking tired. She presented all the cities, but added a slide showing where the campaign was working and a plan to fix the rest. The client was unhappy at first, then asked her to lead the fix. I don't know what she said to the boss. But I know I'd have been tempted to just drop those cities.

qa.q: What did the boss suggest dropping from the presentation?
qa.a: The boss suggested dropping the weakest cities.

qa.q: What might Sarika's long stare at her screen suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was uncomfortable with the request and weighing what to do.

qa.q: Which choice worked here, and why?
qa.a: Presenting all the data honestly with a clear improvement plan kept the client's trust and even won Sarika more responsibility.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see her own likely choice?
qa.a: Sangeeta admits being tempted to give in too, which shows how real the pressure was.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a young analyst report metrics honestly under pressure.

subtype: Conflict of Interest, Data Privacy & Honest Reporting
passage:
Week one: Vikas, a data analyst at a hospital software firm, was asked by a sales colleague for a spreadsheet of patient emails to 'send a friendly offer'. Vikas said he'd check. That night he couldn't sleep.

Week two: He read the company's privacy policy twice and asked his manager, Jasleen. She said clearly that patient data could not be used for sales. Vikas felt relieved, then worried the sales colleague would be annoyed.

Week four: The sales colleague did grumble. But at the next team meeting, Jasleen reminded everyone of the rule without naming anyone. Two other analysts admitted they'd been asked too. Vikas started keeping a small note of every data request he received and who approved it.

qa.q: What did the sales colleague ask Vikas for?
qa.a: He asked for a spreadsheet of patient emails to send a friendly offer.

qa.q: Why couldn't Vikas sleep after the request?
qa.a: He felt uneasy that sharing patient data for sales might be wrong, but he wasn't sure yet.

qa.q: What habit did Vikas build to protect data in future?
qa.a: He began keeping a note of every data request and who approved it.

qa.q: How might the patients be affected if Vikas had shared the emails?
qa.a: Their private details would be used for sales without their consent, which could break their trust in the hospital.

grounding: Shows a young analyst checking the rules and refusing to misuse client data under pressure.

subtype: Conflict of Interest, Data Privacy & Honest Reporting
passage: Charu beta, come. Your Bhupen mama will tell you about his first audit job. I was twenty-five then. A client company was run by my father's old friend. He invited me home for dinner the first week. I went, of course, and he talked about the old days. Later his accountant hinted that some bills could be 'overlooked'. I realised then that the dinner wasn't just kindness. I felt sick. I went to my senior the next morning and told her about the friendship. She moved me to another client. My father was upset with me for a while. But the friend's company was later caught, and I was clean. So when you start at the bank, if someone you know is involved, say so early. On day one, not after the dinner.

qa.q: Who ran the client company in Bhupen's first audit job?
qa.a: His father's old friend ran it.

qa.q: What did Bhupen realise when the accountant hinted that some bills could be overlooked?
qa.a: He realised the friendly dinner may have been meant to influence him, which made him feel sick.

qa.q: What advice does Bhupen give Charu for her bank job?
qa.a: If someone she knows is involved, disclose it early instead of hiding it.

qa.q: How might Bhupen's father have seen his choice at first?
qa.a: He was upset, probably feeling Bhupen had disrespected an old friendship.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how he disclosed a conflict of interest and stayed honest under pressure.

subtype: Conflict of Interest, Data Privacy & Honest Reporting
passage: At 9 pm, with the client presentation at ten the next morning, Ramesh finished the campaign report and felt his stomach sink. Sign-ups were twenty per cent below target. His manager, Yamini, had told the client last week that they were 'on track'. She called from a cab. 'Can we count the newsletter subscribers as sign-ups? Just this once.' They weren't the same thing, and Ramesh knew the client would base next quarter's spending on these numbers. He took a breath. 'I can show both, clearly labelled, with a note on why sign-ups dipped and what we'd change. If we blur them, it'll come out later.' There was a long silence and traffic noise. 'Send me both slides,' she said. He worked till midnight on the explanation. The client was disappointed, but at the end asked Ramesh to join the next planning call.

qa.q: How far below target were the sign-ups?
qa.a: Twenty per cent below target.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh's stomach sink when he finished the report?
qa.a: He realised the real numbers contradicted what his manager had promised the client, which meant pressure to fudge them.

qa.q: What made Ramesh's alternative honest and workable?
qa.a: He offered to show both numbers, clearly labelled, with reasons and a plan, so the truth came with context instead of blurred figures.

qa.q: How might the client have seen Ramesh after the meeting?
qa.a: Disappointed by the numbers but trusting his honesty, which is why they invited him to the next planning call.

grounding: Shows a young analyst reporting campaign metrics honestly under deadline pressure from his manager.

subtype: Conflict of Interest, Data Privacy & Honest Reporting
passage: Kunal's message came on Friday evening: 'Bhavna, you have access to the lab's patient database, right? Could you pull a list of diabetic patients in Vashi? For my meal-plan startup. Just phone numbers.' Bhavna, twenty-five, worked in data operations at a diagnostic lab chain in Navi Mumbai. She liked Kunal, and his idea was good. She also knew those numbers belonged to patients who had trusted the lab with their health. She called him instead of typing. 'I can't. It's not mine to share, and it would be wrong even if nobody found out.' He sounded embarrassed: 'Didn't think of it like that.' On Monday came another test: her manager asked her to join the panel choosing a new software vendor. One bidder was her cousin's firm. She told him first thing, in writing, and stepped off the panel. Two honest choices in three days. She felt tired, and oddly light.

qa.q: What did Kunal ask Bhavna to pull from the database?
qa.a: A list of phone numbers of diabetic patients in Vashi, for his meal-plan startup.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna call Kunal instead of typing a reply?
qa.a: She was fond of Kunal and wanted to refuse kindly and clearly, not leave a cold written no.

qa.q: What did Bhavna handle well about her cousin's firm?
qa.a: She disclosed the conflict at once and in writing, then stepped off the panel, keeping the vendor choice fair.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt after her refusal?
qa.a: Embarrassed, since he had not thought about the patients' trust, but likely able to understand her reason.

grounding: Shows a young professional protecting client data from a friend's request and disclosing a conflict of interest.
